pos: n. (a mass of clay or dough; a cake of figs; rendering Greek phurama, Hebrew debelah)
etymology: Middle English lumpe, a shapeless mass. Paul's word, phurama, is what has been kneaded — dough on the board or clay on the wheel.
biblical_def: Paul uses the lump three ways. Of sovereignty: “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” (Rom 9:21). Of covenant: “if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches” (Rom 11:16). Of discipline: “Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened” (1Co 5:6–7; Gal 5:9). Isaiah's remedy for Hezekiah was “a lump of figs” laid on the boil (2Ki 20:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lump as a small mass of matter of no definite shape; a mass of things blended or thrown together without order.
webster_full: LUMP, n. A small mass of matter of no definite shape; as a lump of earth; a lump of butter.
2. A mass of things blended or thrown together without order or distinction.
3. A cluster; as a lump of figs.
scriptures: Rom 9:21
Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches.
Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?
Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:
Gal 5:9
A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.
And Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs. And they took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered.
corruption_summary: The potter is said to shape vessels according to what the clay has already become, and Paul's whole point is that both vessels come of the same lump.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 9:21 is the verse the doctrine of election has always had to answer for, and the usual escape is to say that the potter makes his choice according to the clay — that the vessel unto honour was foreseen to believe, and the vessel unto dishonour foreseen to refuse. Paul wrote of the same lump to shut that door. There is no difference in the clay. The difference is in the potter's will, and Paul's answer to the objection he knew was coming is not an explanation but a rebuke: “who art thou that repliest against God?” A reader who has never felt the force of that rebuke has not read the verse.

First Corinthians 5 turns the same word on the church. A man had his father's wife, the Corinthians were proud of their tolerance, and Paul's answer was baker's arithmetic: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. Discipline is not cruelty to one member but protection of the batch, and the church that will not put out the leaven because it loves the leavened man has decided to be a leavened lump. The command to purge is grounded in what they already are — “as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” — which is the shape of every New Testament command: become what the cross has made you.
roots_summary: Greek phurama (G5445), that which is kneaded, dough, a lump of clay; Hebrew debelah (H1690), a pressed cake of figs.
roots_lines: Greek phurama (G5445) — a kneaded mass, dough, clay; Romans 9:21, 11:16, 1 Corinthians 5:6–7, Galatians 5:9.
Hebrew debelah (H1690) — a cake of pressed figs; 2 Kings 20:7, Isaiah 38:21, 1 Samuel 25:18.
usage: “Of the same lump” — no difference in the clay.
“A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” — discipline as protection of the batch.
“If the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy” — the root and the branches.

pos: n. and adv. (a hundred times as much; rendering Hebrew me'ah she'arim, Greek hekatontaplasion)
etymology: Hundred + fold, the old English way of multiplying. In the parable it is the yield of good ground; in Mark 10 it is what a man receives who has left everything.
biblical_def: Isaac “sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold: and the LORD blessed him” (Gen 26:12). In the parable the seed on good ground “brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold” (Mat 13:8), and the good-ground hearer is the one “that heareth the word, and understandeth it” (Mat 13:23). To those who have forsaken houses and brethren for His name's sake the Lord promises “an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life” (Mar 10:30; Mat 19:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hundredfold as a hundred times as much.
webster_full: HUNDREDFOLD, n. A hundred times as much.
scriptures: But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.

And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.
But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Then Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold: and the LORD blessed him.
Luk 8:8
And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold. And when he had said these things, he cried, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
corruption_summary: The hundredfold of Mark 10:30 is preached as a return on giving, and the verse lists what the return is and ends with persecutions.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse has been sold harder than Mark 10:30. The prosperity preacher reads “an hundredfold now in this time” and stops; the Lord went on to itemise: houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands — with persecutions. The man who has left his family for Christ receives a hundred families, because every house of the church is open to him; that is the hundredfold, and it is paid in people, not in property, and it comes with persecutions attached. Peter, who asked the question that drew the promise, died with no house of his own and brethren in every city of the empire. He got exactly what was promised.

The parable keeps the number honest from the other side. The hundredfold there is fruit, not return — what the seed produces in the hearer, not what the hearer gets for having heard. Isaac's hundredfold in Genesis 26 is a plain harvest and the text gives its cause in four words, “and the LORD blessed him,” in a famine year, in a land where he had been told to stay by faith. Scripture's hundredfold is always God's doing and never a formula, and the man who sows to get a hundredfold has planted the wrong thing.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'ah she'arim (H3967, H8180), a hundred measures; Greek hekatontaplasion (G1542), a hundredfold; hekaton (G1540), a hundred.
roots_lines: Hebrew me'ah she'arim (H3967 with H8180) — a hundred measures; Genesis 26:12.
Greek hekatontaplasion (G1542) — a hundredfold; Matthew 19:29, Mark 10:30, Luke 8:8.
Greek hekaton (G1540) — a hundred; Matthew 13:8, 13:23.
usage: “An hundredfold now in this time… with persecutions” — paid in people, not property.
“Some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold” — fruit, not return.
“Received in the same year an hundredfold: and the LORD blessed him” — Isaac's harvest in a famine.

pos: v. (to hold within limits; to restrain oneself; rendering Hebrew kul, Greek choreo and egkrateuomai)
etymology: Latin continere, to hold together. Solomon used it of the heaven of heavens and God; Paul used it of a man and his desires.
biblical_def: Solomon at the dedication: “But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?” (1Ki 8:27; 2Ch 6:18). John of the Lord's works: “if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written” (John 21:25). Paul of the unmarried: “if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn” (1Co 7:9). Elijah's trench “would contain two measures of seed” (1Ki 18:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contain as to hold, as a vessel; to comprehend; to restrain; and, intransitively, to live in continence or chastity.
webster_full: CONTAIN, v.t. To hold, as a vessel; as, the vessel contains a gallon.
2. To comprehend; to comprise; to include.
3. To restrain; to withhold from trespass or disorder.
CONTAIN, v.i. To live in continence or chastity.
scriptures: But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
But will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built!
John 21:25
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD: and he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed.
corruption_summary: God is spoken of as contained in a building or a bread, and Solomon said the heaven of heavens could not contain Him on the day he built the house.
corruption_paragraphs: The man who built the temple was the man who said it could not hold God. Solomon's sentence is the guard against every localising of the Almighty since: the shrine where He is more present than elsewhere, the sanctuary that is holy ground while the street is not, the phrase “God showed up” as if He had been away. The Reformed held to the old maxim that the finite cannot contain the infinite, and applied it where it stung — to the claim that the body of Christ is enclosed in the bread of the supper. Stephen quoted Solomon to the Sanhedrin (Act 7:48–49) and was stoned for it, because a religion that owns the place where God is contained does not like to be told that He is not.

First Corinthians 7:9 uses the word of a man's mastery of himself, and the verse is the answer to compulsory celibacy. Paul honours the single state and then sets the limit: if they cannot contain, let them marry. Rome made a vow of what Paul made a gift, and required of every priest what the apostle would not require of any Christian. The result was foreseen in the second half of the verse.
roots_summary: Hebrew kul (H3557), to hold, sustain, contain; Greek choreo (G5562), to have room for; egkrateuomai (G1467), to exercise self-control.
roots_lines: Hebrew kul (H3557) — to contain, hold, sustain; 1 Kings 8:27, 18:32, 2 Chronicles 2:6, 6:18, Ezekiel 45:11.
Greek choreo (G5562) — to make room, contain; John 21:25, Mark 2:2.
Greek egkrateuomai (G1467) — to contain oneself, be temperate; 1 Corinthians 7:9, 9:25.
usage: “The heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” — said by the builder on the day of dedication.
“The world itself could not contain the books” — John's last sentence.
“If they cannot contain, let them marry” — the gift, not the vow.

pos: v. (to be of one mind; to come to terms; to correspond; rendering Greek sumphoneo, eunoeo, and isos, Hebrew ya'ad)
etymology: Old French agreer, to please, from Latin gratus. The chief Greek word, sumphoneo, is to sound together — the root of symphony.
biblical_def: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3). “Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him” (Mat 5:25). “If two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father” (Mat 18:19). The false witnesses at the Lord's trial failed because “neither so did their witness agree together” (Mar 14:59). James at the council: “to this agree the words of the prophets” (Act 15:15). “There are three that bear witness in earth, the spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three agree in one” (1Jn 5:8). And of the ten kings: “God hath put in their hearts to fulfil his will, and to agree, and give their kingdom unto the beast” (Rev 17:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agree as to be in concord; to harmonize in opinion; to come to a settlement; to be consistent; to suit.
webster_full: AGREE, v.i. To be in concord or harmony; to live in peace.
2. To harmonize in opinion or sentiment; to be of one mind.
3. To come to one opinion or mind; to settle by stipulation; as, to agree on a price.
4. To be consistent; to correspond; to suit.
scriptures: Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven.
Mat 5:25

Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.
But neither so did their witness agree together.
And to this agree the words of the prophets; as it is written,
And there are three that bear witness in earth, the spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three agree in one.
corruption_summary: Matthew 18:19 is made a formula for getting anything by prayer in pairs, and the verse sits inside the Lord's instruction on church discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: “If two of you shall agree” has been detached from its chapter and turned into a technique: find a second person, agree on the request, and the Father is bound. Read four verses back. The Lord is describing the steps of discipline — tell him his fault alone, then take one or two more, then tell it to the church — and the agreement of the two is the agreement of witnesses in a judgment; what they bind and loose on earth is bound and loosed in heaven because they are acting in His name, and He is in the midst of them. The verse is a promise to a church exercising the keys, not to two friends wanting a car. Its scope is the Father's will, which is why the same Gospel records the Son praying alone in Gethsemane and not receiving the cup's removal.

Amos 3:3 asks the question ecumenism does not want asked. Two cannot walk together except they be agreed, and the modern instinct is to walk first and hope agreement is unnecessary. Scripture's unity is a unity in something — the faith once delivered — and the false witnesses of Mark 14 are the picture of a fellowship without it: many voices, all against Christ, and none agreeing with another. The three that agree in one in 1 John 5:8 are the model: the Spirit, the water, and the blood bear one testimony because they testify to one truth.
roots_summary: Greek sumphoneo (G4856), to sound together, agree; eunoeo (G2132), to be well-minded toward; isos (G2470), equal, consistent; Hebrew ya'ad (H3259), to appoint, meet by agreement.
roots_lines: Greek sumphoneo (G4856) — to sound together, agree; Matthew 18:19, 20:2, 20:13, Acts 5:9, 15:15.
Greek eunoeo (G2132) — to be well-disposed, agree; Matthew 5:25 only; isos (G2470), consistent; Mark 14:56, 14:59.
Hebrew ya'ad (H3259) — to meet by appointment, agree; Amos 3:3.
usage: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” — the question ecumenism avoids.
“If two of you shall agree on earth” — the witnesses of Matthew 18, not a prayer trick.
“Neither so did their witness agree together” — a fellowship with nothing in common but its target.

pos: n. (a pattern to be copied; a warning instance; rendering Greek hupodeigma, hupogrammos, tupos, and deigma)
etymology: Latin exemplum, a sample taken out. Peter's word for Christ's example is the copybook line a child writes under.
biblical_def: Christ washed the disciples' feet and said, “I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). Peter: “Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps” (1Pe 2:21). Timothy is to “be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity” (1Ti 4:12). The prophets are “an example of suffering affliction, and of patience” (Jas 5:10). The word also warns: Israel in the wilderness is “the same example of unbelief” (Heb 4:11), and Sodom is “set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire” (Jud 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines example as a pattern, in morals or manners, proposed for imitation; a precedent; an instance serving for illustration or warning.
webster_full: EXAMPLE, n. A pattern; a copy; a model; that which is proposed to be imitated.
2. A pattern, in morals or manners; a copy or model; that which is proposed or is proper to be imitated.
3. Precedent; a former instance.
4. A person or thing punished, as a warning to others.
scriptures: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:
John 13:15
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Heb 4:11
Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.
Jud 1:7

Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.
Jas 5:10
Take, my brethren, the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience.
corruption_summary: Christ is reduced to an example, and the verse that calls Him one says in the same breath that He suffered for us.
corruption_paragraphs: The oldest way to lose the gospel is to keep Christ as a pattern and drop Him as a substitute — the moral-influence Christ, who shows men how to live and die and leaves them to do it. First Peter 2:21 will not be read that way. “Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example”: the substitution comes first and the example is left behind it, and three verses later Peter says what the suffering did — “who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.” An example cannot bear sins. The Greek word Peter chose, hupogrammos, is the perfect line of letters at the top of a child's copybook; the child traces it, and he was never going to write it first.

John 13:15 has been made into a third ordinance by some, who wash feet in the assembly as they baptise and break bread. The Lord called it an example, which is the one thing He did not call the bread and the cup. What He commanded was that they do as He had done — the posture of the servant — not that they do what He had done. The church that keeps the basin and forgets the posture has kept the wrong half.
roots_summary: Greek hupodeigma (G5262), a pattern, specimen; hupogrammos (G5261), a writing-copy; tupos (G5179), a type, model; deigma (G1164), a specimen for warning.
roots_lines: Greek hupodeigma (G5262) — an example, pattern; John 13:15, Hebrews 4:11, 8:5, James 5:10, 2 Peter 2:6.
Greek hupogrammos (G5261) — a copybook line to trace; 1 Peter 2:21 only.
Greek tupos (G5179) — a type, pattern; 1 Timothy 4:12, Philippians 3:17, 1 Corinthians 10:6; deigma (G1164), Jude 1:7.
usage: “Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example” — substitute first, pattern second.
“I have given you an example” — the posture, not a third ordinance.
“Set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire” — Sodom as warning.

etymology: From follow, Old English folgian. The Greek behind every AV occurrence is mimetes, an imitator — one who copies, not one who trails behind.
biblical_def: The word is always a command or a commendation. “Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” (Eph 5:1). “Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1Co 11:1; 1Co 4:16). “Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample” (Php 3:17). The Thessalonians “became followers of us, and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction” (1Th 1:6). Hebrews: “be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Heb 6:12). Peter: “who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good?” (1Pe 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines follower as one who comes, goes, or moves after another; an adherent; an imitator; one who takes another as his pattern.
webster_full: FOLLOWER, n. One who comes, goes or moves after another, in the same course.
2. One that takes another as his guide in doctrines, opinions or example; a disciple; an adherent.
3. An imitator; one who copies the example of another.
scriptures: Eph 5:1
Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
And ye became followers of us, and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Ghost:
Heb 6:12
That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
And who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good?
Php 3:17
Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample.
corruption_summary: Be ye followers of me is quoted without its second clause, and the clause is the whole warrant.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul said “be ye followers of me” three times, and the man who quotes it to gather a following has left out the words that made it lawful: “even as I also am of Christ.” The apostle's example was derived, and it was to be followed exactly as far as it was derived and no farther. Every personality ministry since has kept the command and dropped the condition, and the result is a congregation of followers of a man. The opposite error is equally modern: the Christian who will follow no man, on principle, and thereby refuses Hebrews 6:12 and 13:7, which command him to imitate the faith of those who have gone before. Scripture's word is imitator. An imitator copies a pattern; he does not join a fan club.

First Thessalonians 1:6 shows what following looks like when it is real: they became followers “having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Ghost.” What was copied was not Paul's manner but Paul's suffering and Paul's joy, and the copy was so exact that in verse 7 the copiers had become the pattern — “so that ye were ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia.” That is how the word is meant to propagate: from Christ to the apostle, from the apostle to the church, from the church to the next church, each generation an imitation of the one before and all of them of Him.
roots_lines: Greek mimetes (G3402) — imitator; 1 Corinthians 4:16, 11:1, Ephesians 5:1, 1 Thessalonians 1:6, 2:14, Hebrews 6:12, 1 Peter 3:13.
Greek summimetes (G4831) — fellow-imitator; Philippians 3:17 only.
usage: “Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ” — the condition that makes the command lawful.
“Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” — imitation as sonship.
“Followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” — the dead worth copying.

pos: v. (to keep hold of; to keep in possession; rendering Hebrew tamak, chazaq, and kala, Greek krateo and echo)
etymology: Latin retinere, to hold back, keep. The word turns on a grip: what the hand keeps, or the mind will not keep.
biblical_def: Job's wife: “Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die” (Job 2:9). Solomon's father: “Let thine heart retain my words: keep my commandments, and live” (Pro 4:4). “A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches” (Pro 11:16). “There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death” (Ecc 8:8). The risen Lord to the apostles: “Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained” (John 20:23). And Paul on the descent of the Gentile mind: “even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines retain as to hold or keep in possession; to keep, as an associate; to keep back; to hold from departure.
webster_full: RETAIN, v.t. To hold or keep in possession; not to lose or part with or dismiss.
2. To keep, as an associate; to keep from departure.
3. To keep back; to hold.
4. To hold from escape.
scriptures: John 20:23
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.
Rom 1:28
And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;
Job 2:9
Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.
Pro 4:4
He taught me also, and said unto me, Let thine heart retain my words: keep my commandments, and live.
Ecc 8:8

There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it.
A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches.
corruption_summary: John 20:23 is made the charter of priestly absolution, and Romans 1:28 shows that unbelief is a refusal to retain, not a failure to find.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome reads John 20:23 as the ordination of a confessional: the priest hears, weighs, and forgives or withholds. The apostles never did any such thing. Not one of them in Acts hears a private confession and pronounces a private absolution; what they do is preach — “through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: and by him all that believe are justified” (Act 13:38–39) — and by that preaching sins are remitted to the believing and retained to the unbelieving, and the church by its discipline declares which is which. The power is declarative, and it is exercised on the terms of the gospel, not the discretion of a man. A minister who tells the impenitent he is forgiven has not remitted anything; he has lied about the terms.

Romans 1:28 locates unbelief in the will. The Gentiles “did not like to retain God in their knowledge” — they had Him, in the things that are made, and they let go of Him on purpose because they did not like the grip. The modern unbeliever presents himself as a man who searched and could not find; Paul describes a man who found and would not keep. The verse's consequence is the most frightening in the chapter: God gave them over. Judgment on the refusal to retain God is being permitted to succeed at it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamak (H8551), to grasp, hold fast; chazaq (H2388), to hold strongly; kala (H3607), to restrain, hold back; Greek krateo (G2902), to hold fast; echo (G2192), to have, hold.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamak (H8551) — to grasp, keep hold; Proverbs 4:4, 11:16, 3:18.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to hold fast; Job 2:9; kala (H3607), to restrain; Ecclesiastes 8:8.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold, retain; John 20:23; echo (G2192), to have, keep; Romans 1:28.
usage: “Whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained” — declared on the gospel's terms, not a priest's.
“They did not like to retain God in their knowledge” — unbelief as a let-go, not a failed search.
“Dost thou still retain thine integrity?” — the question meant to break a grip.

pos: n. (a word sent by one person to another through a bearer; rendering Hebrew dabar and mal'akut, Greek aggelia and presbeia)
etymology: Old French message, from Latin missus, sent. A message is not the messenger's own; John's word for it, aggelia, is what an angel carries.
biblical_def: John twice names the content of the apostolic message: “This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1Jn 1:5); and “this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another” (1Jn 3:11). Haggai was “the LORD's messenger in the LORD's message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD” (Hag 1:13). Ehud told Eglon, “I have a message from God unto thee,” and it was a dagger (Jdg 3:20). The citizens in the parable “sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us” (Luk 19:14). “He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage” (Pro 26:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines message as any notice, word, or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.
webster_full: MESSAGE, n. Any notice, word or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.
2. An official written communication of facts or opinions sent by a chief magistrate to the two houses of a legislature.
scriptures: This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
Hag 1:13
Then spake Haggai the LORD'S messenger in the LORD'S message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD.
Jdg 3:20
And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat.
But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.
Pro 26:6
He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, and drinketh damage.
corruption_summary: The modern message begins with man's needs, and the apostle's message began with a sentence about God.
corruption_paragraphs: First John 1:5 is the first thing the apostles had to say, and it is not about the hearer. “This then is the message… that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” The felt-needs gospel opens with the man — his wounds, his potential, his search — and brings God in afterward as the answer to what the man was already asking. John opens with God's character, and everything that follows in the letter (walking in the light, confessing sin, the blood that cleanses) is the consequence of that one sentence. A message that starts anywhere else will end somewhere else.

The word itself is a correction. A message is carried, not composed; Haggai was the LORD's messenger in the LORD's message, and the whole of his authority was that the words were not his. The preacher who improves the message has become its author, and the citizens of Luke 19 show what men do with a message they dislike: they send one back. “We will not have this man to reign over us” is the reply of every generation to the announcement of a King, and the parable records what the King did when he returned.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word, matter; mal'akut (H4400), a message, errand; Greek aggelia (G31), a message, announcement; presbeia (G4242), an embassy.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, message; Judges 3:20, 1 Kings 20:12, Proverbs 26:6.
Hebrew mal'akut (H4400) — a message, errand; Haggai 1:13 only.
Greek aggelia (G31) — message, announcement; 1 John 1:5, 3:11; presbeia (G4242), an embassy; Luke 19:14, 14:32.
usage: “This then is the message… that God is light” — the apostles' first sentence.
“The LORD's messenger in the LORD's message” — carried, not composed.
“Sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us” — the reply of the citizens.

pos: adj. (bringing no gain; useless; rendering Greek achreios, achrestos, anopheles, and alusiteles)
etymology: Un + profitable, from Latin proficere, to make progress. The Lord used the word of two servants, and only one of them was cast out.
biblical_def: Two servants are called unprofitable. The one who hid his talent: “cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Mat 25:30). And the one who did everything: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). Paul says of all men, “they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one” (Rom 3:12); of Onesimus, “in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me” (Phm 1:11); of foolish questions and strivings about the law, “they are unprofitable and vain” (Tit 3:9). Hebrews warns that grieving one's pastors “is unprofitable for you” (Heb 13:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unprofitable as bringing no profit; producing no gain beyond the labor and expense; useless; serving no purpose.
webster_full: UNPROFITABLE, a. Bringing no profit; producing no gain beyond the labor, expenses and interest of capital.
2. Producing no improvement or advantage; useless; serving no purpose; as unprofitable servants.
scriptures: So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Rom 3:12
They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one.
Phm 1:11
Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me:

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
corruption_summary: Rome teaches works of supererogation, and the Lord told the servant who had done everything to call himself unprofitable.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 17:10 is the grave of merit. The servant in the parable has ploughed, fed cattle, come in, girded himself, and served his master's supper — done all those things which are commanded — and the Lord's instruction is that he say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which was our duty to do. The doctrine of supererogation holds that a man may do more than God requires and bank the surplus for others; the verse holds that a man who has done everything required has produced no surplus at all, because duty was owed. The Confession puts it in the Lord's own words: when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty, and are unprofitable servants. Grace is not what God gives to the servant who exceeds his duty. It is what He gives because none does.

Matthew 25:30 is the other unprofitable servant, and the contrast is exact. The one who did all and called himself unprofitable is commended; the one who did nothing and was called unprofitable by his lord is cast into outer darkness. Faithfulness does not earn, and idleness is not safe. Paul's Onesimus is the word's happiest use: a runaway slave, unprofitable to his master, made profitable by the gospel and sent back with a letter — the only kind of profit Scripture is finally interested in.
roots_summary: Greek achreios (G888), useless, unprofitable; achreioo (G889), to become useless; achrestos (G890), unserviceable; anopheles (G512), unprofitable; alusiteles (G255), not paying.
roots_lines: Greek achreios (G888) — useless, unprofitable; Matthew 25:30, Luke 17:10 only.
Greek achreioo (G889) — to become unprofitable; Romans 3:12; achrestos (G890), Philemon 1:11.
Greek anopheles (G512) — unprofitable; Titus 3:9, Hebrews 7:18; alusiteles (G255), Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” — the grave of merit.
“Cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness” — the other servant, who did nothing.
“In time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable” — Onesimus.

pos: n. and v. (worth; to estimate the worth of; rendering Hebrew arak, Greek diaphero and timao)
etymology: Old French value, from Latin valere, to be strong, to be worth. In Leviticus it is the priest's estimate; in Matthew it is what a man is worth to God against sparrows, and what Christ was worth to the priests against silver.
biblical_def: “Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows” (Mat 10:31; Luk 12:7). Job to his comforters: “ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value” (Job 13:4). In the law of vows “the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, who art the priest, so shall it be” (Lev 27:12). And Matthew, on the thirty pieces: “they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value” (Mat 27:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines value as worth; that property of a thing which renders it useful or estimable; and, as a verb, to estimate the worth of; to rate.
webster_full: VALUE, n. Worth; that property or those properties of a thing which render it useful or estimable; or the degree of that property or of such properties.
2. Price; the rate of worth set upon a commodity.
VALUE, v.t. To estimate the worth of; to rate at a certain price.
2. To esteem; to hold in respect and estimation.
scriptures: Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.
Luk 12:7
But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.
Mat 27:9
Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;
Job 13:4
But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value.
And the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, who art the priest, so shall it be.
corruption_summary: Human worth is preached as a possession a man carries in himself, and Matthew 10 grounds it in a Father who counts sparrows.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-esteem gospel and Matthew 10:31 agree that a man is of great value and disagree about where the value lives. The modern doctrine locates it inside the man, as a dignity he owns and must learn to feel. The Lord locates it in the Father's attention: not one sparrow falls without Him, the hairs of your head are numbered, therefore fear not — you are worth more than many sparrows to the One who counts sparrows. Value in Scripture is conferred, not discovered; it is the price the Owner sets, and the verse was given to men about to be delivered up to councils and scourged, as the reason they need not fear. A dignity that comes from inside would not have helped them.

Matthew 27:9 records the valuation the other way. The chief priests, who knew the law of vows and the price of a slave, valued the Son of God at thirty pieces of silver — the sum Exodus 21:32 sets for a gored slave — and Zechariah had already called it “a goodly price that I was prised at of them” with the irony intact. Every man values Christ at something, and the price he sets is the truest statement of his own worth he will ever make.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak (H6186), to arrange, estimate, value; elil (H457), worthless, of no value; Greek diaphero (G1308), to differ, surpass in value; timao (G5091), to set a price on.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H6186) — to estimate, value; Leviticus 27:8, 27:12, 27:14.
Hebrew elil (H457) — worthless, nothing; Job 13:4, “physicians of no value.”
Greek diaphero (G1308) — to be of more value; Matthew 10:31, 12:12, Luke 12:7; timao (G5091), to value; Matthew 27:9.
usage: “Ye are of more value than many sparrows” — worth set by the One who counts sparrows.
“The price of him that was valued” — thirty pieces, the price of a gored slave.
“Physicians of no value” — Job's comforters.
